messages.subject: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
parts:
Hello,

The focus of my study is to compare species assemblages and abundances
across different habitats - i.e. relative abundance. My fieldwork was
conducted in a region in PNG where no abundance studies have been underta=
ken
before. As a result I was unsure what time would be best suited for varia=
ble
circular plots. To hedge my bets and make the most of my limited time I
spent 20mins recording detections but broke these up into 5 minute interv=
als
so I now have a record of birds and the times they were detected.=20

Of course, the issue with doing such a long survey means that there is an=

increased risk in violating assumption 2: That objects are detected at
their initial location.
This is especially the case in my habitats which were very in dense tropi=
cal
rainforests.

I was wondering if it would be legitimate to truncate the records accordi=
ng
to time and species? For some species, we know that they can sit for up t=
o
and over 20mins without calling and for others we know that they call
frequently and loudly and move around a lot. In the first case I'd keep a=
ll
records up to 15-20mins but for the second species, I'd feel motivated to=

cut off all records after 5-10mins to reduce errors. Would this be
legitimate? I would keep the truncation times constant for a species acro=
ss
habitats. If so, I'm assuming that problems would lie in the judgment cal=
ls
for prolonging the recording time of one species over another.=20

Finally, I've read some papers which argue that the number of birds flyin=
g
into the survey area (and being detected) is equal to the number of that
species flying out of the area without detection - which could make all t=
his
truncation redundant. However, I'm not sure if I necessarily agree with
this, given my observations of this region over the past 3 years.

Sorry for the long-winded query! Thanks for your patience and assistance.=

Kindest regards
Liz

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
parts:
Hi Liz,

Your suggestion of different times tailored to each species sounds good
to me - although remember that the ideal is a snapshot type approach, as
detailed in the Intro to Distance Sampling book and the 2006 paper by
Steve Buckland in the Auk (copy available at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf
). If you can't do a snapshot, make the time interval as short as
possible such that you are sure to count all birds for that species at
or close to zero distance.

I'd like to hear which papers claimed that you expect equal number of
birds flying into the survey area and being detected as flying out
without detection -- this is clearly nonsense, for two reasons: (1)
because the area of an annulus of fixed width goes up linearly as you go
away from a point, there are far more birds available to fly in than
are inside to fly out; (2) after a while you will detect most birds
inside your circle, so there are basically no undetected birds left to
fly out, while on the other hand all birds flying in are available to be
detected. Because of these issues you will always over-estimate
abundance with a longer count time if birds are at all mobile and g(0)=1.

I suspect, as with many multi-species surveys, that sample size will be
an issue for you for many species, and that you'll need to look at
pooling detection functions (and inference) across species (see for
example the 2007 Journal of Applied Ecology paper by Matt Alldredge and
coauthors).

Cheers,

- Len

--

messages.author: 7915d3b1c6db79b6
messages.subject: Re: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
parts:
Liz,
I am sure some of the more experienced statisticians will reply to this
in due time. A quick question first? Did you record distances to the
birds? It was not explicitly stated in your post. I think the
truncation you propose in the third paragraph is dangerous. The problem
you describe as I read it sounds like an availability issue, i.e. birds
are not available to be detected perhaps because of low calling rates.
Can the birds not be detected by sight? If you have models that generate
estimates of availability for each species then you could use them as a
"multiplier" within Distance, but this will only add a level of
complication to your analysis. I think I would be tempted to just use
the first 5 minutes of your survey for the Distance analysis. Truncating
your time-to-detection times /ad hoc/ violates some assumptions.
Another option would be to use another type of analysis such as
occupancy or time-to-detection/removal models. I am less familiar with
the latter, but they may allow you to use all of your data. However, I
think you will still run into issues because your 5-minute intervals are
temporally correlated, and not independent as you have described them.

jm

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
parts:
Hi James and Liz (and list)

I had assumed that distances were being collected, so this was a
distance sampling question. I advised choosing the shortest time so
that g(0)=1 (ie no availability issue). But James has a point -- if
this is too long, so that movement is now an issue, one may wish to try
the time-to-detection methods. Problem there is that, just as with all
capture-recapture type methods, this is negatively biased by un-modelled
heterogeneity in detection prob. Distance is one of the major sources
of heterogeneity, so one may consider combined
time-to-detection/distance sampling methods. These are relatively new,
and still under development. For a brief review of related issues and
methods, see

Nichols, J.D., L. Thomas and P.B. Conn. 2008. Inferences about landbird
abundance from count data: recent advances and future directions. Pp
203-238 in Thomson, D.L., E.G. Cooch and M.J. Conroy (Eds.) Modeling
Demographic Processes in Marked Populations. Environmental and
Ecological Statistics Vol 3. Springer. ISBN: 978-0-387-78150-1

Copy available at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/NicholsEURING2008.pdf

- Len

messages.author: ab53bf182021b795
messages.subject: Re: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
parts:
Hi Len, James and Ben,

Firstly, thank you very much for the replies and the references - extremely helpful.

Yes, I did measure distances - my query was already so long I just didn't expressly state it!

The question really is how to I manage to get g(0) = 1 without increasing time to the point where I violate assumption 2. The best method I could think of was to do it by species, or groups. My biggest difficulty is that the vegetation is so dense and the canopy so high in many of my sites that there's a chance I'm not detecting everything at 0m - even species that call frequently can be hard to detect at the top of a 60m canopy with dense understorey (esp. nectarinia spp.). Yet others will have a low call rate, or will tend to reduce their rate depending on how many conspecifics/congeners are in close proximity (I have found this especially with Ducula spp.) so increasing time ensures their detection within the plot.

I think the advice to keep times short is an excellent one. I'll have a closer look at how my detection distances change over time for each species and see how this affects my decision-making for cut-offs. Ben, that Marsden paper is fantastic - thank you.

In addition to 'normal' VCP survey technique I also recorded those birds which I either knew or suspected had flown in from outside the plot (I'd heard them earlier in the survey in the the same direction outside the plot, I saw them fly in etc.). I call these my OHP records (flew overhead and perched in my site) - they're for use in other presence/absence analysis. I think they may also be useful as a measure of species' movement over time and distance and can assist with determining optimal cut-off times for species.

I'm keen to continue with DISTANCE rather than pioneer in the time-to-detection methods as this is only a part of a much larger project involving local community attitudes to the development in the region I'm surveying. That said, I will investigate these methods and thank you very much for bringing them to my attention.

Len, I'll have a scrounge around for the papers but I read them a number of years ago while studying in the US and they stuck in my brain. They were focusing on the idea of a 'snapshot' and used easily detectable birds to test how many flew in and out of a plot over time. In think in one paper their focal species were highly motile. That said, I can't agree more with the idea that bird availability within a site is far less than without. I suspect they were not measuring distances to the birds.

Thanks again,
Liz


******************************************
Liz Pryde
PhD Candidate
School of Earth and Environmental Sciences
James Cook University, Qld
Australia
******************************************

messages.subject: Re: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
parts:
Hi Len, James and Ben,

Firstly, thank you very much for the replies and the references - extremely helpful.

Yes, I did measure distances - my query was already so long I just didn't expressly state it!

The question really is how to I manage to get g(0) = 1 without increasing time to the point where I violate assumption 2. The best method I could think of was to do it by species, or groups. My biggest difficulty is that the vegetation is so dense and the canopy so high in many of my sites that there's a chance I'm not detecting everything at 0m - even species that call frequently can be hard to detect at the top of a 60m canopy with dense understorey (esp. nectarinia spp.). Yet others will have a low call rate, or will tend to reduce their rate depending on how many conspecifics/congeners are in close proximity (I have found this especially with Ducula spp.) so increasing time ensures their detection within the plot.

I think the advice to keep times short is an excellent one. I'll have a closer look at how my detection distances change over time for each species and see how this affects my decision-making for cut-offs. Ben, that Marsden paper is fantastic - thank you.

In addition to 'normal' VCP survey technique I also recorded those birds which I either knew or suspected had flown in from outside the plot (I'd heard them earlier in the survey in the the same direction outside the plot, I saw them fly in etc.). I call these my OHP records (flew overhead and perched in my site) - they're for use in other presence/absence analysis. I think they may also be useful as a measure of species' movement over time and distance and can assist with determining optimal cut-off times for species.

I'm keen to continue with DISTANCE rather than pioneer in the time-to-detection methods as this is only a part of a much larger project involving local community attitudes to the development in the region I'm surveying. That said, I will investigate these methods and thank you very much for bringing them to my attention.

Len, I'll have a scrounge around for the papers but I read them a number of years ago while studying in the US and they stuck in my brain. They were focusing on the idea of a 'snapshot' and used easily detectable birds to test how many flew in and out of a plot over time. In think in one paper their focal species were highly motile. That said, I can't agree more with the idea that bird availability within a site is far less than without. I suspect they were not measuring distances to the birds.

Thanks again,
Liz

Liz Pryde

School of Earth and Environmental Sciences
James Cook University, Qld
Australia
